title: Waves in Pipes & Strings — 50 MCQs
description: Topics: stationary waves in open/closed pipes, harmonics & overtones, end correction, transverse wave velocity on strings, vibration laws of fixed strings, and related numericals/concepts.

questions.q: A stationary wave in a pipe is formed when:
options: Only one progressive wave is present
Two progressive waves of same frequency travel in opposite directions and superpose
questions.explanation: Standing waves form by superposition of two equal-amplitude, equal-frequency opposite-traveling waves (reflections create the opposing wave in a pipe).

questions.q: In a pipe open at both ends the boundary condition is:
options: Displacement antinode at each open end
Displacement node at each open end
Pressure antinode at each open end
Both ends behave identically to closed ends
questions.explanation: Open ends allow maximum particle displacement (displacement antinodes) and minimum pressure variation (pressure nodes).

questions.q: In a pipe closed at one end and open at the other the allowed harmonics are:
questions.explanation: Closed–open (one end closed) pipes support only odd harmonics: f_n = n v / (4L) with n = 1,3,5,...

questions.q: Frequency of the nth harmonic in an open-open pipe of length L is:
questions.explanation: Open-open pipe supports all harmonics with f_n = n v/(2L) (n = 1,2,3,...).

questions.q: First overtone of an open pipe means:
questions.explanation: The first overtone is the next mode above the fundamental (first harmonic), i.e., the second harmonic.

questions.q: In a open pipe (both ends open) the allowed frequencies are:
questions.explanation: Closed-closed behaves like open-open for allowed modes: nodes at ends produce f_n = n v/(2L).

questions.q: End correction for an open pipe of radius r is approximately:
questions.explanation: Empirical end correction ≈ 0.6 r (for a circular tube) added to physical length for effective acoustic length.

questions.q: Effective length L_eff of an open pipe (both ends open) with physical length L and radius r (small) is approximately:
questions.explanation: Two open ends each contribute ≈0.6 r correction, so L_eff ≈ L + 0.6r + 0.6r = L + 1.2 r.

questions.q: For a string fixed at both ends the fundamental frequency f1 is given by:
questions.explanation: For a string fixed at both ends, λ1 = 2L, so f1 = v/λ1 = v/(2L).

questions.q: Transverse wave speed on a stretched string depends on tension T and linear mass density μ as:
questions.explanation: Transverse wave speed = sqrt(tension / linear mass density).

questions.q: If the tension in a string is quadrupled and μ is constant, wave speed changes by factor:
questions.explanation: v ∝ √T so quadrupling T multiplies speed by √4 = 2.

questions.q: Overtones for a fixed string are:
options: Integer multiples of the fundamental frequency
questions.explanation: Harmonics (overtones) of fixed-fixed string are integer multiples: f_n = n f1.

questions.q: A closed pipe of length L supports a fundamental frequency f1 = v/(4L). What is the next supported frequency?
questions.explanation: Closed at one end supports odd harmonics: next is 3 v/(4L) (n=3).

questions.q: Which of these is true about harmonics and overtones in an open-open pipe vs a closed-open pipe?
options: Open-open: both even & odd harmonics; Closed-open: odd harmonics only
Open-open: odd only; closed-open: even only
questions.explanation: Open-open supports all integer harmonics; closed-open only odd multiples of fundamental.

questions.q: For a string of length L, fixed at both ends, the third harmonic has wavelength:
questions.explanation: For n-th harmonic λ_n = 2L/n → λ3 = 2L/3.

questions.q: If a pipe open at both ends resonates at fundamental 256 Hz, its 4th harmonic frequency is:
questions.explanation: 4th harmonic is n=4: f4 = 4×256 = 1024 Hz.

questions.q: End correction arises because:
options: Air at open end oscillates and effective antinode is slightly outside geometric end
questions.explanation: Open end does not act as exact antinode; air outside vibrates, shifting effective acoustic length beyond physical end.

questions.q: A pipe of length 0.85 m is open at both ends. Taking v = 340 m/s and ignoring end correction, fundamental frequency is approximately:
A string of length 0.5 m with wave speed 200 m/s has fundamental frequency:
If linear mass density μ of a string doubles while T unchanged, fundamental frequency changes by factor:
questions.explanation: v = √(T/μ) decreases by 1/√2, so f1 ∝ v decreases by 1/√2.

questions.q: Which boundary condition corresponds to a closed end of an air column?
questions.explanation: Closed end prevents particle motion ⇒ displacement node; pressure fluctuates maximally ⇒ pressure antinode.

questions.q: Relative ordering closed organ pipe: Fundamental, first overtone, second overtone correspond to which harmonics?
questions.explanation: Fundamental = 1st harmonic; first overtone = 3rdd harmonic; second overtone = 5th harmonic.

questions.q: A closed-open pipe with fundamental frequency 170 Hz has next overtone at roughly:
questions.explanation: Only odd harmonics: f1=170, next is 3×170=510 Hz.

questions.q: For a thin circular pipe of radius r, which has greater end correction constant c (L_eff = L + c r)?
options: Open end into free space: c ≈ 0.6
Small aperture with flange: lower correction
questions.explanation: Standard empirical c ≈ 0.6 for unflanged open pipe; flanged/open geometry can change correction (flanged ≈0.85). The option reflects typical unflanged value.

questions.q: Two pipes of same length: one open-open, one closed-open (one end). Which has lower fundamental frequency (assuming same v)?
questions.explanation: Closed-open fundamental f_closed = v/(4L) which is half of open-open f_open = v/(2L). So closed-open has lower f.

questions.q: If a string vibrates in its 5th harmonic (n=5), how many nodes (excluding end nodes) are present along its length?
questions.explanation: In n-th harmonic there are n-1 internal nodes (excluding fixed end nodes). For n=5, internal nodes=4.

questions.q: A musician shortens a vibrating string by pressing at a fret at 1/3 of its length from one end. The new fundamental frequency relative to original is approximately:
questions.explanation: New length = 2/3 L, so f_new = v/(2×(2/3) L) = (3/2) v/(2L) so f_new = 3/2 f_old.

questions.q: Which statement about an open organ pipe and an open string is correct regarding nodes/antinodes correspondence?
options: Open pipe ends = displacement antinodes; open string (free) similar but string fixed ends are nodes
Open pipe ends are nodes of displacement
questions.explanation: Open pipe ends allow maximal particle displacement (antinode). Strings are typically fixed at ends (nodes), different from open pipe.

questions.q: If wave speed on a string v=100 m/s and string length L=0.8 m, frequency of 3rd harmonic is:
A pipe open at one end and closed at other has fundamental 85 Hz. What is the frequency of its 5th mode (n=5)?
questions.explanation: Closed-open supports odd harmonics: f_n = n v/(4L). If f1=85 → n=5 gives f5 = 5×85 = 425 Hz.

questions.q: End correction becomes more significant when:
options: Radius is not negligible compared to length
questions.explanation: End correction ~0.6 r; for short pipes or large r relative to L, correction is significant.

questions.q: If string linear density μ = 0.01 kg/m and tension T = 100 N, wave speed is:
For a string fixed at both ends, wavelengths allowed are given by λ_n = 2L/n. Which n gives shortest wavelength?
questions.explanation: As n increases wavelength λ_n = 2L/n decreases; largest n gives shortest λ (within physical limits).

questions.q: If a flute (open-open) and a clarinet (approx. closed-open) have same physical length, which sounds lower for same excitation?
questions.explanation: Closed-open fundamental is half frequency of open-open for same L (v/(4L) vs v/(2L)), so clarinet-like tube has lower pitch (approx one octave lower) for same length.

questions.q: Which of these is true for an open-open pipe harmonic series compared to closed-open pipe series?
options: Open-open includes consecutive integers; closed-open includes odd-only giving different timbre
Closed-open gives all even harmonics only
questions.explanation: Open-open supports all integer harmonics; closed-open only odd harmonics — affecting harmonic content and timbre.

questions.q: A pipe open at both ends of physical length 0.6 m has radius 0.01 m. Using end correction, effective length is L_eff ≈ L + 1.2 r. What is L_eff (m)?
When a string vibrates, energy is primarily stored as:
options: Kinetic energy of moving elements and potential energy due to tension (elastic)
questions.explanation: Oscillating string stores KE in particle motion and PE in elastic deformation (due to tension).

questions.q: Which law relates node positions and wavelength for stationary waves on a string fixed at both ends?
questions.explanation: Adjacent nodes are separated by λ/2 on standing waves.

questions.q: If a string length is L and speed v, frequency of second harmonic (n=2) is:
questions.explanation: f_n = n v/(2L); for n=2, f2 = 2 v/(2L) = v/L.

questions.q: A pipe resonates at 400 Hz as its third harmonic (open-open). Fundamental frequency is:
questions.explanation: If 400 Hz is 3rd harmonic, f1 = 400/3 ≈133.33 Hz.

questions.q: Which practice shortens effective vibrating portion of a string raising pitch?
questions.explanation: Shortening string length increases fundamental frequency (f ∝ 1/L), raising pitch.

questions.q: In practice, real organ pipes have end corrections because:
options: Air beyond geometric end participates in oscillation
questions.explanation: Air just outside the open end moves with the internal air, shifting the effective node slightly outside geometric end.

questions.q: If a pipe open at both ends of length L resonates at frequency f, and temperature increases raising sound speed v, the resonant frequency:
questions.explanation: f_n = n v/(2L); if v increases with temperature, f increases proportionally.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a reason for frequency change when a string is tightened?
options: Linear mass density μ changes instantly
questions.explanation: Tension T change is the direct reason; μ normally unchanged unless string material changes. Option lists correct effect; pick the one 'NOT'—if μ changes instantly usually not; but as asked, μ does not change by tightening, so that option is NOT a reason.

questions.q: The nth overtone corresponds to which harmonic number?
questions.explanation: n-th overtone is the (n+1)-th harmonic (first overtone = second harmonic).

questions.q: A pipe of length L closed at one end and open at other has its first three resonant wavelengths as:
questions.explanation: Closed-open supports odd harmonics: wavelengths λ_n = 4L/n with n =1,3,5 → λ1 = 4L, λ3 = 4L/3, λ5 = 4L/5.

questions.q: If a string has frequency 440 Hz at T1 tension, increasing tension to 1.44 T1 yields frequency approximately:
Which is correct about overtone numbering in closed-open pipes?
options: Overtones correspond to odd harmonics only, so first overtone = 3rd harmonic
questions.explanation: Closed-open supports odd harmonics; first overtone is next mode: 3rd harmonic (n=3).

questions.q: A practical consequence of different harmonic series between instruments is:
questions.explanation: Different harmonic content changes instrument timbre even if fundamentals match.

questions.q: Which boundary condition is true for a string attached at one end and free at other (not typical instrument case)?
options: Fixed end = displacement node; free end = displacement antinode
questions.explanation: Fixed end enforces zero displacement (node); free end allows maximal displacement (antinode).
